items.item: The orphan rule: an impl is allowed only if the trait or at least one of its types is defined in the current crate

items.item: The orphan rule exists to guarantee coherence: exactly one impl of any trait for any type can ever exist, program-wide

at.deep: Internals: coherence, GATs, and why the orphan rule exists

items.item: The real distinction isn't that associated types are 'less flexible' than generic parameters; it's that a generic parameter makes the trait itself parameterized, so Trait<A> and Trait<B> are different trait bounds that can each be independently implemented for the same Self type

at.step: A generic parameter dodges that limit

items.item: A duplicate impl failure (E0119) has nothing specifically to do with associated types; it is coherence's blanket rule that a type gets exactly one impl of a given trait, period, and an associated type simply gets fixed inside whichever one impl exists

at.step: Can the same type pick Output twice?

items.item: A GAT's lifetime parameter is resolved per call, not per impl, which is exactly what std::iter::Iterator's plain associated Item cannot express, because Item has no lifetime parameter of its own to tie to a single &mut self borrow

at.step: An item that borrows from the call itself

items.item: The orphan rule is not primarily about preventing the author's own mistakes; it's about making a dependency upgrade safe: two crates adding the same foreign-for-foreign impl independently would silently conflict the moment both ended up in one dependency graph

at.step: Implementing a foreign trait for a foreign type

items.item: The newtype pattern doesn't change what the orphan rule allows; it changes which type the impl is for, substituting a genuinely local type for the foreign one, so the exact same rule now accepts it

at.step: A local wrapper satisfies the rule

items.item: A blanket impl is itself subject to the orphan rule like any other impl; std's own impl<T: Display> ToString for T is only legal because ToString is defined in std, the same crate as the blanket impl itself

at.step: One impl, every type that qualifies

items.item: Specialization (letting a more specific impl override a blanket one) would let two impls of the same trait for an overlapping set of types coexist, which is exactly the coherence property the orphan rule and the one-impl-per-type rule both exist to prevent on stable Rust today

An async fn in a trait needs a hidden, compiler-generated Future type per implementation, which is itself a kind of per-impl associated type the compiler invents automatically — a reason it interacts with this topic's whole subject even though the full mechanism is out of scope here

Coherence is checked once, at compile time, for the whole crate graph being built; it is not a run-time property and never causes an ambiguous method call to be resolved differently depending on which code path reaches it first

at.deep: Internals: coherence, GATs, and why the orphan rule exists

items.item: Fundamental types (like Box<T> or references) are treated specially by coherence: the T inside Box<T> is not counted as 'covered', so Box<LocalType> counts as local even though Box itself is foreign, which is why wrapping in Box (rather than a newtype) does not generally satisfy the orphan rule the same way a plain newtype does
